After its peak at \$5,318 per ounce in January, gold price has dipped to about \$4,000 right now, marking a 
drawdown of about 25%. Because gold is 
non-yielding (i.e. holding it does not generate any interest), the opportunity cost of holding
gold is the interest a saver could earn by lending to the government. 
Given recent increase in yield on 10-year Treasury Inflation-Protected Securities (10Y TIPS),
which is a Treasury bond whose principal adjusts to inflation and rise in energy price,
the drop in gold price seems reasonable. 
Yet, when we zoom out a little, the price of gold has actually doubled since 2021,
while the 10Y TIPS rate rose 3.6 percentage points.
This seems to contradict the theory that there is an inverse
relationship between gold and the real interest rate.

Other factors seem to dominate the movement, at least periodically. 
Usually, there are three candidates other than real interest rate: dollar, stocks, and oil.
I regress gold's weekly return on all four at once, so each number
below is one factor's effect with the other three held fixed.
This post tries to answer: which of these exposures does the price of gold carry and how big is
each? Understanding the correlations and movements can be
important to central banks, especially those in the emerging market, as they divert away
from U.S. government bonds and dollars when Russian accounts were frozen. Knowing
which risk gold actually carries is also
pertinent to anyone who wishes to invest in assets with relatively stable long-term return,
since gold is a precious physical good with inherent value and no credit risk. 

## Gold's exposure to dollar, real yield, stock, and oil
The interactive figure below gives a rolling sensitivity analysis of gold against other factors, with
a two-standard-error confidence band. Click the dropdown menu to select the factor/asset. 

- **Dollar**. Over the past twenty years, for every 1% increase in dollar index, gold price drops by
1.6% on average. The exposure remains negative and has barely exceeded 0 even for the upper bound of the interval.
There is a very clear and persistent negative link between dollar and gold.
- **Real yield**.A one-point rise in the 10-year real yield lowers gold by 3.5% with the dollar held fixed. Real yields and the
  dollar usually rise together, though. If we count the stronger dollar that comes with real yield, a one-point rise has gone
  with a 6.3% fall in gold. The link between real yield and gold is rather unstable as the two-year estimate swings from -14 to +6.
- **Stock**. Before 2022, a 1% fall in the S&P 500 came with a 0.2% rise in gold, making
gold a weak hedge. Since 2022, the estimate is zero. This makes sense as commodities have historically
exhibited low correlation with equities. 
- **Oil**. The direct exposure of gold to oil is close to zero in every window. Yet, energy price shock
affect gold price indirectly through real yields and dollar. Before 2026 oil did not move real yields, 
but in 2026 an oil jump pushed real yields and the
  dollar up, and gold fell about 1% for every 10% rise in Brent.
- **Drift**. There is also the return none of the four factors explains, which
is about 11% a year before 2022 and 21% since. Figure 3 will return to it.

## Is gold still a safe asset?

Figure 2 plots gold's monthly total returns against three types of portfolio. The rust dots are the 
the worst 10% of months for a portfolio, and the blue dots are the rest of the months. When we hover over
the dots, we can see the return for both in each month. The dropdown menu allows us to select each portfolio. 
For the portfolio
with 60% stock ETF and 40% Treasuries, the average return in the worse 10% of the month is -4.4%. In those months gold 
averaged -0.9% and rose 48% of the time, below its usual 55%. 
If we switch the dropdown to pure S&P500 ETF, before 2022 gold rose in 76% of the worst equity months, 
and since 2022 in only 2 of 8 (too few sample to draw any conclusion yet).
Finally, for the pure bond portfolio, gold fell 2.9% on average in the worse Treasury months.
The rate exposure from Figure 1 is showing up exactly when bonds lose money.

<iframe src="fig2_bad_months.html" width="100%" height="580" style="border:none;" loading="lazy" title="Figure 2: monthly gold returns against a 60/40 portfolio, stocks, or bonds"></iframe>

*Figure 2. Monthly total returns from month-end prices, February 2003 to October 2026*

## Where the returns actually came from

Figure 3 decomposes the contribution of each of the factors to gold's yearly return. 
The colored pieces are what the four exposures account
for, and grey is the unexplained factor. We could hover over the bars to see
the detailed decomposition. Clicking a legend
entry can remove a component and allows us to see what remains.

In the past five years, the unexplained
factor accounts for a significant proportion of gold's return. In 2024 and 2025,
the grey bar is about twice the size of any year before 2022.In 2022, real yields and dollar both rose, and they together contributed to -17
log points to gold's return. However, gold price ended flat because the 
the drift added +13 points, offsetting the downward pressure from higher
yields and stronger dollar. 

More strikingly, in 2024, gold rose 27% against the backdrop of stronger dollar, and +44
log points was due to the unexplained factor. 2025 continued the trend, with 
the drift contributing 55 points. 

<iframe src="fig3_decomposition.html" width="100%" height="560" style="border:none;" loading="lazy" title="Figure 3: contributions to gold's yearly return"></iframe>

*Figure 3. Each factor's contribution is its full-sample coefficient x the factor's cumulative move that
year, in log points so the pieces add up to the year's return*

## What might the drift be?

There are many candidate explanations for the drift, and the post is only
making a tentative approach to explain two of the candidates. First, 
central banks bought more than 1,000 tonnes of gold
a year in 2022-24, over twice their 2010-21 average of 473.[^wgc24] Central bank 
is a buyer who ignores TIPS yields and the dollar, so Central Bank purchase raises 
gold’s average return without changing how gold reacts to those factors. The increase
in purchase from central banks was probably due to security reasons, as the G7 froze 
Russia's account and imposed a series of sanctions after the outbreak of war. This is why
it was mainly central banks from emerging markets that were making the purchases.

Second, 
gold ETFs took in 801 tonnes[^wgc25] in 2025 when central banks buying
slowed to 863 tonnes. This signifies that investors flow started to support gold as well. 
As such, the main driver of the drift was central bank purchase from 2022-2024, and 
2025 was a combined force from both investors and central banks. 

[^wgc24]: World Gold Council, *Gold Demand Trends: Full Year 2024*, central banks section: 2024 was the third consecutive
year above 1,000 tonnes, against an annual average of 473 tonnes in 2010-2021.
<https://www.gold.org/goldhub/research/gold-demand-trends/gold-demand-trends-full-year-2024/19411>

[^wgc25]: World Gold Council, *Gold Demand Trends: Full Year 2025*, central banks section (net purchases 863 tonnes; 2024
revised to 1,092 tonnes) <https://gold.org/goldhub/research/gold-demand-trends/gold-demand-trends-full-year-2025/central-banks>;
ETF inflows of 801 tonnes as reported in "Gold demand tops 5,000 tonnes for the first time", *Graphic Online*, 1 February 2026.

## Caveats

- Gold and the four factors react to the same news, so this post only analyzes the comovement/correlation and not
  causation
- The post-2022 samples are relatively short. There are 251 weeks for the regressions, and only 8 to 13 bad months in each part of the
  hedge test.

## Takeaway

Holding gold is first a bet against the dollar (1.6% per 1%, steady for twenty years) and second a bet against real
yields (6.3% per point, half of it through the dollar). Oil enters only through those two, and there is
not direct link between oil and gold. Gold has not been be a reliable insurance for a
60/40 portfolio because it rose in 48% of the worst months and falls when bonds fall. And since 2024 these exposures explain
none of its rise in gold. The 120% came from a drift that prices alone cannot explain, and that turned negative in 2026.
What changed after 2022 is not how gold reacts to the dollar or real yields, which is about the same before and
after, but the drift, which doubled, and the weak stock hedge, which disappeared.

## Data and code

- Gold: COMEX gold futures, front-month continuous contract (`GC=F`), daily close in US dollars per troy ounce; Yahoo Finance via `yfinance`
- Stocks: SPDR S&P 500 ETF (`SPY`), dividend-adjusted; Yahoo Finance via `yfinance`
- Bonds: iShares 7–10 Year Treasury ETF (`IEF`), dividend-adjusted; Yahoo Finance via `yfinance`
- Real yield: 10-year Treasury inflation-indexed constant-maturity yield (`DFII10`, Federal Reserve Board H.15); FRED
- Dollar: nominal broad trade-weighted dollar index (`DTWEXBGS`, Federal Reserve Board); FRED
- Oil: Brent crude spot (`DCOILBRENTEU`, U.S. Energy Information Administration); FRED

Daily data from 2 January 2003 to 22 October 2026, accessed 24–25 October 2026. The four-factor regressions start in
January 2006, when the dollar index begins.

Method: the regressions use weekly (Friday-to-Friday) changes with Newey–West standard errors; Figure 1 uses a two-year
(104-week) rolling window. Figure 2 uses monthly total returns from month-end prices; the 60/40 portfolio is 60% SPY and
40% IEF, rebalanced monthly, and the worst months are those at or below each portfolio's 10th-percentile return.
Figure 3 multiplies each factor's full-sample coefficient by the factor's cumulative move in each year.

Code, data and every number quoted above: [github.com/1iiiiii/Gold-vs.-Real-Yield](https://github.com/1iiiiii/Gold-vs.-Real-Yield).
